title: How to respond to a zestimate objection on Mac, with scripts for realtors
metaTitle: How to respond to a zestimate objection: realtor scripts
description: Respond to a Zestimate objection by checking Zillow's accuracy data, the home facts it uses, and days on market. Scripts for buyers and sellers.
secondaryKeywords: how to handle a Zillow estimate
intro: To respond to a Zestimate objection, agree that the number is an estimate, then ask what the client is comparing it to. Then show the facts behind your price, using Zillow's own accuracy figures and recent local sales. The goal is a calm conversation about one home, not a debate about one website.
tldr: Agree that the Zestimate is an estimate, not an appraisal or an offer, then ask what the client compared.
Zillow's own learn page gives a 1.77% median error for on-market homes and 7.20% for off-market homes, dated 2022.
Redfin's analysis links overpricing to 3 to 4 months on market, versus 1.5 to 2.5 months for accurate pricing.
Check the home facts Zillow uses before the call, then bring recent local sales that really match the home.
Lazur can explain what is on screen, point at it, and draft your reply, but it does not verify the numbers for you.

blocks.text: What a Zestimate objection sounds like

A Zestimate objection is any pushback that leans on Zillow's estimate. The client says the home is worth more, or less, because Zillow says so. Sometimes it is a buyer arguing for a lower offer. Sometimes it is a seller who will not accept a list price below the number on the screen.
The objection is rarely about software. It is about trust. The client wants to know whether you have seen the same numbers, and whether your price still holds when they check it themselves.
Start with what Zillow says about its own accuracy

Zillow publishes its own accuracy figures on a learn page. For on-market homes, the nationwide median error is 1.77%. For off-market homes, it is 7.20%. The page is dated April 13, 2022, and it does not say which period the rates cover. Quote the numbers, but quote the date too.

Median error is not the same as average error. A median is the middle value in a set of results. Half the estimates miss by less than the median, and half miss by more. That is useful context, but it does not tell you which homes are far off.

Zillow also says that for on-market homes in major metros, the Zestimate is within 20% of the selling price more than 99% of the time. Read that carefully. A 20% band is wide. It can hold a price well above or below what a buyer will pay. Zillow itself notes that accuracy depends on how much local data is available.
Check the facts the estimate is built on

The estimate is only as good as its inputs. Zillow says it uses public property and tax records, recent local sales, and user-submitted information. It also says the formula uses hundreds of data points for each home. If one input is wrong, the estimate is wrong too.

blocks.caption: Where the Zestimate's inputs come from, and how to check them before a call
rows: Lot size, bedroom count, bathroom count, year built

Renovations with dates, and any permitted work

Dates and prices for past sales on the home
The sale history section on the Zillow home page

blocks.text: Work through this table before the call, not during it. A short check on the facts can save a long argument. If a fact is wrong, Zillow's advice is to claim the home and edit it. If work was done without a record, Zillow suggests telling the tax assessor about it.
A script for a buyer who quotes Zillow
Buyers usually quote the Zestimate to argue for a lower offer. Do not start by defending your price. Start by agreeing that the number is a real data point, then ask what they are comparing it to.

Try this: “That’s a fair thing to look at. What did you see on the page, and which home were you comparing?” Listen for the answer. Often the buyer is comparing a different size, condition, or street. The buyer may also have a point about one fact, which you can check.

Then bring one sold comparable that matches the home closely. Walk through why it matters, one feature at a time. If something has changed since the estimate's data was recorded, name it. Keep the conversation on this home, not on Zillow.
A script for a seller who wants a higher price

Sellers who quote the Zestimate often treat the number as a floor. Your job is to show where the estimate could be off in either direction. Start with facts the seller already knows, such as a new roof or a finished basement.

Try this: “Zillow is a useful starting point. Its own page says accuracy depends on local data. Here are the sales that closed nearby recently, and here is how each one compares.” Then stop talking. Let the seller react before you add anything.

If the seller still wants a higher price, ask what would change their mind. Ask it kindly. A clear answer gives you something to test, such as a price review after a few weeks of showings or feedback.
Mistakes people make in this conversation

items: Arguing the Zestimate's accuracy in general terms instead of the one home in question.
Quoting a median error without saying it is a median, or leaving out the 2022 date.
Calling the client wrong. Ask questions first, and let the facts do the work.
Promising a quick sale when the data does not guarantee timing.
Ending the call without a written summary, so the same objection returns next week.

blocks.text: When the Zestimate is closer than you think

Sometimes the estimate is right, or closer than your gut. A home with few recent local sales is hard to value for anyone, including you. New construction, unusual lots, and homes in thin markets are common examples. Zillow says accuracy depends on how much local data exists.

Renovations cut both ways. Work done without permits, or without a record, may not appear in public data. The estimate then misses real value. A recent kitchen update may be worth more than the record shows, and a buyer may already expect to pay for it.

blocks.title: Fix the fact first
blocks.text: If the estimate shows the wrong bedroom count, the wrong lot size, or a sale that never happened, correct the fact before you discuss the price. Do not argue with a number you can fix.
What time on market tells you

Redfin's March 2026 analysis ties pricing accuracy to time on market. Sellers priced 5 to 10% above accurate value spent 3 to 4 months on market on average. Accurately priced sellers sold in 1.5 to 2.5 months. Underpriced sellers sold in about one month or less.

Use this with care. The analysis is correlational, and it does not name the dataset behind the figure. Still, it gives you a plain way to frame risk. Ask the client what it costs to wait several extra months, and let them answer in their own terms.

blocks.title: Correlation is not proof
blocks.text: A pattern in Redfin's data does not prove that a specific home will sit. Present it as a risk to weigh, not as a promise about the sale.
What the research says and what it leaves out

A working paper from NBER, issued in March 2022 and revised in June 2023, studies Zillow's Zestimate. Its authors, Fu, Jin and Liu, find that listing and selling outcomes respond significantly to the estimate. They also find that disturbances are short lived. The paper is about feedback in the market, not about agent conversations.

A separate federal rule covers automated valuation models. Its quality control standards took effect October 1, 2025, for banks and other regulated institutions that use these models. It does not govern a Zestimate quoted at a showing, so treat it as background, not as a rule for agents.

No peer reviewed study we checked tests whether a Zestimate anchors buyers or sellers in a negotiation. Anchoring is a known idea in negotiation, but the Zestimate version is untested in the sources we found. Treat it as a plausible cause, not a measured one.
The survey behind the price objection numbers

A survey by Lone Wolf and Giant Steps Advisors covered 2,165 real estate professionals from 46 states. Nearly two-thirds of them named price as the top seller objection. The Inman article does not give an exact percentage, so do not quote one.

The same survey found that 91% of respondents trust MLS data most, and fewer than 1% trust public portals. The article says more clients use Zillow data to argue that their agent's price is too low. It does not mention Zestimates by name, so treat the link as likely, not proven.
How Lazur helps during the conversation

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. That helps when a Zillow page is open in front of a client and you need the sale history or the facts section explained.

Ask Lazur to point. It draws a circle and a label around the element on screen, so you can show a client exactly which fact you mean. Ask it to walk you through a fact edit, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You still do the clicking.

For replies, hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That suits a follow-up email in Gmail after a call. Lazur can also draft text and type it at your cursor. You read the draft, change what is wrong, and send it yourself.

For background, Lazur can run a research job in its own Chrome tabs and return a summary and a report. Use it to gather public context, then check every number against your MLS and brokerage tools before a client sees it. Research does not replace that check.
What Lazur will not do here

Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It does not send emails on your behalf, and it does not pull your MLS data. It cannot confirm that a Zestimate is right. It can explain what is on screen, point at it, guide you through a step, and draft words you review.
Client data and your brokerage rules

Realtors handle personal information about buyers and sellers. Before you paste a client's name, address, or offer details into any AI tool, check your brokerage and state rules. Your employer's policy comes first. If you are unsure, describe the situation without the client's details.

When you hold the shortcut, Lazur sends the audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer. Lazur's privacy note says those are not stored, and that content is never used to train AI models. Read the note yourself, and know what is on screen before you hold the shortcut.
Build a comparable sales sheet in Google Sheets

A short sheet beats a long argument. Create columns for address, sale date, sale price, days on market, bedrooms, bathrooms, square feet, and a notes column for condition. Sort by sale date with Data > Sort range, then remove any sale that is not truly similar.

Format price cells with Format > Number > Currency. Format any change column as a percent with Format > Number > Percent. Keep notes short, such as “renovated kitchen” or “corner lot,” so you can read them aloud on a call.
Prepare your Mac for a live call

Open Chrome with the Zillow page, your sales sheet, and your MLS tab before the call starts. Use ⌘ 1, ⌘ 2 and ⌘ 3 to jump between tabs. Keep the sales sheet in its own window so you can show it without hunting.

If you share your screen in Zoom, share one window, not the whole desktop. Close personal messages and anything that shows other clients first. A pop-up in the middle of a price argument breaks the room.
After the call, write it down

Keep the written summary to three parts. First, the one fact that changed. Second, the comparables you used, with one line each. Third, the question the client agreed to think about. Short summaries are easier to answer, and easier to reread before the next call.

faq.question: What should I say first when a client quotes a Zestimate?
faq.answer: Agree that the number is a starting point, then ask one question. Ask what the client compared. That keeps you from arguing the number before you know what they saw. A calm question works better than a rebuttal.

faq.question: Is the Zestimate accurate enough to rely on?
faq.answer: Zillow's learn page gives a nationwide median error of 1.77% for on-market homes and 7.20% for off-market homes. The page is dated April 13, 2022, and it does not say what period the rates cover. A median is not an average, and no single figure applies to one home.

faq.question: Should I tell a client the Zestimate is wrong?
faq.answer: Say so only when you can point to a specific fact, such as a missing renovation or a wrong bedroom count. Show the fact, explain its effect, and let the client check it. Do not call the estimate useless.

faq.question: Can I paste client details into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your brokerage and state rules first, and follow your employer's policy. When you hold ⌥ ⌘, Lazur sends the audio and screenshot to AI providers to answer. Lazur's privacy note says they are not stored and not used for training.

faq.question: Does Lazur pull MLS data or confirm the Zestimate?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains what is on screen, points at it, and can run research in its own Chrome tabs. Confirm every number against your MLS and brokerage tools before a client sees it.

faq.question: Can I run the Zillow Premier Agent app on my Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's App Store listing says the app is designed for iPad and not verified for macOS. The listing gives macOS 13.0 or later and an Apple M1 chip or later as requirements. Check the listing before you rely on it.

costs.title: Time spent on the wrong argument
costs.text: Every minute spent defending a Zillow number is a minute not spent on the offer, the showing, or the next client. HousingWire reports that Realtors worked a median of 35 hours a week in 2025. Your time is already tight, so spend it where you control the outcome.

costs.title: A listing that sits longer
costs.text: Redfin's analysis links overpricing to longer stays on the market. Sellers priced 5 to 10% above accurate value averaged 3 to 4 months on market. Accurately priced homes sold in 1.5 to 2.5 months. The data is correlational, so treat it as a warning, not a promise. Each extra week is still a cost your seller feels.

costs.title: Price cuts that come later
costs.text: A Redfin article dated June 26, 2026 says about 20.2% of active US listings had reduced their asking price. Those cuts averaged 4.0%. If an argument over a Zestimate pushes a listing above the market, the later cut is a cost you may have avoided.

costs.title: Trust with the client
costs.text: When a client trusts a portal over you, the work turns into a debate about software. The Inman survey found that 91% of respondents trust MLS data most, and fewer than 1% trust public portals. Your strongest case uses MLS data, the source most respondents trust.

costs.title: Credibility when a fact is wrong
costs.text: If the estimate shows a wrong bedroom count or misses a renovation, and you do not catch it, you lose the argument on the facts. Clients remember who was wrong. Check the record before you respond.

causes.title: The number looks official
causes.text: Zillow shows one figure in a clean box, which looks like a measurement. The Zestimate uses public property and tax records, recent local sales, and user-submitted information. Zillow says the formula uses hundreds of data points for each home. A single number built from many inputs feels precise, even when it is an estimate.

causes.title: Public records can lag behind the house
causes.text: Public records update on their own schedule. Work done without a permit, or without a record, may not appear at all. Zillow's advice to owners is to tell the tax assessor about unrecorded work. Until that happens, the estimate can miss real value in either direction.

causes.title: Thin local data in some areas
causes.text: Zillow says accuracy depends on how much local data is available. In a neighborhood with few recent sales, the estimate leans on fewer inputs. That caveat sits on Zillow's learn page, not in the number itself, so most clients never read it.

causes.title: A feedback loop between estimates and sales
causes.text: A working paper by Fu, Jin and Liu, issued in March 2022, finds that listing and selling outcomes respond significantly to the Zestimate. The estimate reacts to sales, and sales react to the estimate. The paper finds that disturbances are short lived.

causes.title: Portals reach the client first
causes.text: The Inman article says more clients now use Zillow data to argue that an agent's price is too low. This is a survey finding, not a count of clients. The number often reaches the client before you do, so the conversation starts from their screen.

causes.title: Anchoring on the first number
causes.text: Once a number is on screen, people tend to use it as a starting point. Anchoring is a known idea in negotiation. The research we checked does not test it for Zestimates, so treat it as a likely cause, not a measured one.

fixes.title: Read Zillow's accuracy page first
fixes.text: Open zillow.com/learn and read the section on accuracy. Note the on-market median error of 1.77% and the off-market error of 7.20%. Also note the April 13, 2022 date and that the page does not say which period the rates cover. Quote the figures with their limits, not as a verdict.

fixes.title: Check each fact the estimate uses
fixes.text: Find the home on Zillow and read the facts it lists. Compare bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, lot size, and year built against the county record and your own visit notes. Zillow's advice to owners is to claim the home and edit its facts when they are wrong.

fixes.title: Check the sale dates on the home
fixes.text: Zillow says owners can check the sale dates shown on the site. A sale that is recorded late or wrongly can shift the picture. Pull the sale history, and note any sale that does not match the listing history.

fixes.title: Build a short comparables list
fixes.text: Pick the sales that match the home most closely, and explain each match in one line. Use your MLS for these sales, not a portal, because most survey respondents trust MLS data most. Keep the list short enough to read on a call.

fixes.title: Ask what would change their mind
fixes.text: Ask the client which fact, sale, or condition would make them accept your price. Write the answer down. If the answer is nothing, the issue is not the estimate. The issue is the decision to buy or sell at that price.

fixes.title: Offer a review date instead of a debate
fixes.text: If the client still disagrees, agree on a date to review activity, showings, or feedback. Put the date on the calendar. A review date turns an argument into a test both sides can see.

fixes.title: Send the facts in writing the same day
fixes.text: Email the facts you covered, the comparables you used, and the one question the client agreed to consider. A written summary keeps the objection from returning as a new argument next week.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Read the estimate
plan.text: Open Zillow's learn page and read the accuracy section. Write down the on-market and off-market median errors and the date on the page. Practice saying each figure with its limits in one sentence.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Audit the facts
plan.text: Check the facts for the homes you list or show most often. Compare bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, and renovation dates with the county record and your notes. Fix what is wrong where Zillow allows edits.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build the sales sheet
plan.text: Open Google Sheets and list recent similar sales with address, sale date, price, days on market, and notes. Sort with Data > Sort range. Keep only the sales that truly match the home.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write two short scripts
plan.text: Write one buyer script and one seller script. Start each by agreeing the estimate is a data point. End each with one question about what the client compared.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Rehearse and log the calls
plan.text: Rehearse one script out loud with a colleague on Zoom, or dictate it with fn. After each real call, note which objection came up and which fact settled it. Review those notes on Friday.
